The flight of the Nationalist government of the Republic of China from the mainland to the island of Taiwan in 1949, after it lost the Chinese Civil War to the Communists. Chiang Kai-shek moved his capital to Taipei in December 1949, two months after Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic in Beijing.

Soldiers, officials, their families and other refugees followed: estimates run from about one to two million people. They brought the Kuomintang party, a large army, the gold reserves and much of the old imperial art collection, now in the National Palace Museum. Taiwan had been a Japanese colony from 1895 to 1945, and the newcomers ruled over the island's majority under martial law until 1987.

The split has lasted. Two governments still claim the name China, and Taiwan's status is one of the most dangerous questions in world politics. It was not the first such retreat: in 1661 the Ming loyalist Koxinga had also crossed to Taiwan to fight on against a new dynasty.
